summary: Outlines a framework for using Robust Header Compression over IPsec security associations, compressing the inner headers to reduce overhead while keeping IPsec's protection. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Encrypting traffic adds bytes to every packet. This memo describes a way to remove some of those bytes: compress the packet headers inside the encrypted tunnel before they are encrypted, and expand them again at the far end.

questions: how does rohc work over ipsec
why does ipsec add overhead to packets
subtitle: Compressing the headers inside an IPsec tunnel to cut the cost of encryption.

tldr.problem: IPsec protects traffic but adds overhead to every packet, and that overhead is costly on links that are short of bandwidth, especially for small packets.
tldr.mechanism: The framework puts Robust Header Compression at the two ends of an IPsec security association instead of on every link, compressing the inner IP and transport headers before encryption and expanding them after decryption.
tldr.outcome: Two companion documents are needed to make it work: IKEv2 extensions that negotiate the compression parameters and IPsec extensions that carry the new state and the protocol identifier.

today: RFC 5856 is an Informational document published by the IETF in May 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets out a framework and points to two companion documents, RFC 5857 and RFC 5858, for the IKEv2 and IPsec extensions that it needs.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document outlines a framework for integrating Robust Header Compression, ROHC, over IPsec, called ROHCoIPsec. The goal is to reduce the protocol overhead associated with packets travelling between the two ends of an IPsec security association. This is achieved by compressing the transport layer header, such as UDP or TCP, and the inner IP header of packets at the ingress of the IPsec tunnel, and decompressing those headers at the egress.

The framework assumes that ROHC will be used to compress the inner headers of IP packets traversing an IPsec tunnel. Current ROHC specifications detail its operation on a hop-by-hop basis, so extensions are needed to let it operate over IPsec security associations. The framework targets tunnel mode associations. Transport mode associations protect only the payload of an IP packet and leave the IP header untouched, and intermediate routers use that header to route the packet to the decryption device, so compression there could apply only to the transport layer headers. Since the current ROHC specifications do not support compression of transport layer headers alone, the framework described here applies to tunnel mode associations.
sections.plainLanguage: ROHC normally works between neighbouring devices on one link. Here it is moved to the two ends of an encrypted tunnel, so the compressed headers stay compressed all the way across the network.

sections.title: Problem Statement: IPsec Packet Overhead
sections.content:
IPsec provides security services for IP networks, but its benefits come at the cost of increased per-packet overhead. Traffic flow confidentiality, generally used at security gateways, requires tunnelling IP packets between IPsec implementations. The tunnel masks the source and destination patterns an intruder could otherwise see, but it costs bytes: an Encapsulating Security Payload tunnel mode security association applied to an IPv6 flow results in at least 50 bytes of additional overhead per packet.

That overhead is undesirable on wireless and satellite networks that are not overprovisioned. ROHC applied on a per-hop basis over such links also suffers reduced performance when encryption is used on the tunnelled header, since encrypted headers cannot be compressed. Packet overhead matters most for traffic profiles with small payloads, such as various voice codecs, because the same fixed cost is added to every small packet.
sections.plainLanguage: An encrypted tunnel wraps each packet in more headers. For an IPv6 flow that is at least 50 extra bytes on every packet, which is a lot when the payload is a single voice frame.

sections.title: Overview of the ROHCoIPsec Framework
sections.content:
ROHC reduces packet overhead by exploiting the redundancy between the headers of packets in the same flow. The framework is built on three assumptions: ROHC is used to reduce the overhead of unicast IP packets traversing an IPsec security association; ROHC is instantiated at the two ends of the association and applied on a per-association basis; and once decompression completes, the recovered headers are identical to the original headers.

Because ROHC now operates between two endpoints across many intermediate nodes that are transparent to the security association, its performance can be affected by packet reordering or loss between the compressor and the decompressor. ROHC can also no longer rely on the underlying link layer for channel parameter configuration and packet identification, so the framework proposes that channel parameters are configured by a security association management protocol such as IKEv2, while identification of compressed packets is done with the Next Header field of the security protocol header, either AH or ESP.

On the outbound path, the implementation compresses the appropriate packet headers and then encrypts and integrity protects the packet. For tunnel mode associations, compression applies to the transport layer and inner IP headers. On the inbound path, the device first decrypts and integrity checks the packet, then decompresses the inner headers, and then checks the packet against the access controls applied to all inbound traffic on that association.

Compression of the inner headers is independent from compression of the security protocol and outer IP headers, which ROHC profiles already handle on a hop-by-hop basis. If IPsec NULL encryption is applied, ROHC may still compress the inner headers at the ends of the tunnel, but that poses a challenge for intermediary devices such as traffic monitors and sampling tools that inspect the contents of such packets; policies on those devices may need to be updated so that packets carrying the ROHC protocol identifier are not dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressor sits at the entrance to the tunnel and the decompressor at the exit. Each is told by the security association itself which traffic to compress, and the security protocol header records whether a given packet is compressed or not.

sections.title: How the Two Ends Process Packets
sections.content:
The framework adds two decisions to the standard IPsec processing model, and the same two apply to outbound and inbound traffic.

The first decision uses a new item of state, the ROHC data item, held in the security association database entry. It decides whether the traffic is handed to the ROHC module at all. Packets on an association where ROHC is disabled follow normal IPsec processing and must not be sent to the ROHC module; packets on an association where ROHC is enabled must be sent to it.

The second decision decides whether the packet can be compressed. If it can, an integrity algorithm may be used to compute an Integrity Check Value for the uncompressed packet, the Next Header field of the security protocol header must be populated with the ROHC protocol identifier, the inner packet headers must be compressed, and the computed value may be appended to the packet. If the packet will not be compressed, the Next Header field must carry the appropriate next-level protocol value and no ROHC processing is applied. On the inbound path the decision is made from the Next Header field: if it does not indicate a ROHC header the decompressor must not attempt decompression, and if it does, the decompressor decompresses, then may compute an integrity value for the decompressed packet and compare it with the value computed at the compressor. The packet is forwarded if they match and dropped if they do not.

With a single association between the compressor and the decompressor, ROHC must operate in unidirectional mode. With a pair of associations, it may operate in bi-directional mode, where the pair represents one bi-directional ROHC channel. If the ROHC protocol requires bi-directional communication, two associations must be instantiated: one for the compressed traffic and one for the feedback, which matches the way IKE creates associations in pairs. An implementation must relay feedback received on the inbound association to the compressor on the corresponding outbound association.

Channel parameters can be set manually for manually managed associations or negotiated by IKEv2. The Next Header field is used to separate compressed traffic from uncompressed traffic on an association where ROHC is enabled, because a compressor may support only a limited number of compressed flows, or a flow may arrive for which no ROHC profile has been signalled. IANA has allocated the value 142 to ROHC in the Protocol ID registry, and that identifier is only defined for use in the Next Header field of security protocol headers.

Two further points are covered. ROHCv2 profiles include mechanisms that give more robustness over reordering channels, and these should be adopted. A decompressor may use the IPsec sequence number to recognise a packet as sequentially late, which improves the chance of decompressing a reordered packet. Feedback from the decompressor to the compressor should be minimised, because any feedback must itself be processed by IPsec and tunnelled back; the alternatives are to operate in unidirectional mode only, or to piggyback feedback messages on the traffic that already travels on the feedback association.

An additional integrity check may be applied before compression, to protect the original IP header. ROHC is designed to tolerate random loss and reordering, but it does not guarantee that a packet rebuilt at the decompressor is identical to the original, and a malicious reordering attack is not the same as random loss. The extra check ensures that erroneous packets are not forwarded into the protected domain. Path maximum transmission unit issues also arise, because ROHC headers can be larger than the headers they replace and an integrity value adds bytes, so the resulting packet can exceed the path MTU in the unprotected domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries a marker saying whether its headers are compressed. The receiver unpacks the headers, checks them against a value computed before packing, and drops the packet if they disagree. The parameters of the compression are agreed when the association is set up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations associated with ROHCoIPsec can be mitigated by using a strong integrity-check algorithm to ensure the valid decompression of packet headers.

A malfunctioning or malicious compressor at the ingress of the tunnel can send erroneous packets to the decompressor that do not match the original packets emitted by the end hosts. This may reduce efficiency between the two, or cause the decompressor to forward erroneous packets into the protected domain. A malicious compressor could also generate a large number of compressed packets, which may cause denial of service at the decompressor, because decompressing many invalid packets drains the resources of the device.

A malfunctioning or malicious decompressor can disrupt communications as well. It may simply discard a subset of the packets it receives, or all of them, even when the headers were validly decompressed, which may result in denial of service. A malicious decompressor could also deliberately report that its context is not synchronised with the compressor's context, forcing the compressor back to a lower compression state and reducing the efficiency that ROHCoIPsec would otherwise deliver.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends of the tunnel can misbehave. A compressor that sends bad packets can waste the decompressor's resources, and a decompressor that drops packets or pretends to be out of step can stop the traffic or undo the savings.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: All IANA considerations for ROHCoIPsec are documented in the two companion documents: RFC 5857, which specifies the IKEv2 extensions to support Robust Header Compression over IPsec, and RFC 5858, which specifies the IPsec extensions. The framework summary in Section 6.2 lists what is needed to achieve ROHCoIPsec: the IKEv2 extensions and the IPsec extensions, and nothing else.
sections.plainLanguage: The number assignments and the detailed formats live in two other documents, one for the key exchange and one for IPsec itself.

viz.caption: WHERE THE COMPRESSED HEADERS SIT IN AN ENCRYPTED PACKET

layers.label: Transport and inner IP headers
layers.detail: Compressed together by ROHC between the two ends of the tunnel

layers.label: ROHC
layers.detail: Robust Header Compression, applied per security association

layers.label: ESP or AH
layers.detail: Encrypts and protects the compressed packet

layers.label: Outer IP header
layers.detail: Carries the packet across the unprotected network

viz.caption: THE PARTS OF THE ROHC OVER IPSEC FRAMEWORK

items.title: ROHC data item
items.text: New state held per security association that says whether the traffic is compressed at all.

items.title: Next Header field
items.text: Carries the ROHC protocol identifier, value 142, so the receiver knows when to decompress.

items.title: Integrity Check Value
items.text: Computed before compression and checked after decompression, so a rebuilt packet can be confirmed.

items.title: Channel parameters
items.text: Set by hand or negotiated with IKEv2 when the association is created.
